title: Japanese chicken curry
skill: Roux with curry powder, from scratch

notes.text: For more than 8, you'll need a very big pot, at least 8 quarts, and a few more minutes for the potatoes to soften.

move.title: A brown roux with curry
move.body: A roux is butter and flour cooked together, and it thickens liquid into a sauce. Today you'll cook a roux longer than usual, until it's light brown and nutty, then stir curry powder into it and use it to thicken a pot of chicken, carrots, and potatoes into mild Japanese curry over rice. In Japan, most people buy curry blocks, but many of them contain animal fats we don't use, so this one is made from scratch.

why.title: Longer cooking, deeper flavor
why.body: A pale roux tastes mild. Cooked slowly a few more minutes, the flour toasts and the roux turns the color of peanut butter and smells nutty. That toasty flavor is what makes Japanese curry taste rich. Go slowly: a roux can burn in seconds once it's brown.

why.title: Blooming the curry powder
why.body: Curry powder is a mix of ground spices, and their flavor dissolves in fat, not water. Stirring the powder into the hot butter roux for half a minute wakes the spices up, so they taste warm and full instead of dusty.

why.title: Loosen the roux first
why.body: A spoonful of thick roux dropped into a big pot of broth can stay in lumps. Whisking a ladle of broth into the roux first makes a smooth, pourable paste that mixes right in.

why.title: A little sweet, a little salty
why.body: Japanese curry is gently sweet. Honey and ketchup add sweetness and a little tang, and soy sauce adds saltiness and depth. Together they balance the spices.

wrong.sign: The roux has black flecks or smells burnt
wrong.fix: Start the roux over. Burnt roux makes the whole curry bitter.
Whisk it hard right in the pot for a minute. Small lumps melt as it simmers.
Stir in a little broth or water until it's how you like it.
Simmer with the lid on a few more minutes, stirring the bottom so nothing sticks.

quiz.q: Why stir the curry powder into the hot roux?
choices: Spice flavor comes out in hot fat
quiz.explain: Spices bloom in hot fat. That's why so many curries start with spices in oil or butter.

quiz.q: What color should this roux be?
quiz.explain: Cooking the roux longer toasts the flour and gives the curry its rich flavor.

steps.text: Put the rice in the saucepan and cover it with cold water. Swish it with your hand, then carefully pour off the cloudy water, holding the rice back with your hand. Do this 3 times.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes off loose starch, so the rice cooks up fluffy instead of gluey.

steps.text: Chop the onions. Peel and mince the garlic. Scrape the skin off the ginger with the edge of a spoon and grate it on the small holes of the grater. Peel the carrots and potatoes and cut them into bite-size chunks, the carrots a little smaller.
steps.tip: Carrots are harder than potatoes, so smaller pieces finish cooking at the same time.

steps.text: Heat the oil in the large pot over medium heat. Add the onions and cook, stirring now and then, until soft and golden.
While the onions cook, cut the chicken into 1-inch pieces and leave it on the cutting board.
Wash your hands with soap. Leave the chicken on the board for now.
steps.tip: Raw chicken can carry germs. Wash before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Add the garlic and ginger to the onions and stir for 30 seconds. Slide the chicken in from the board with the back of the knife, and stir until it's white on the outside.
Wash your hands, the knife, and the cutting board with hot, soapy water.
steps.tip: Raw chicken can carry germs. Wash before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Add the carrots, potatoes, broth, and {qty:salt} salt. Bring it to a boil, then turn the heat down, put the lid on, and simmer until the potatoes are tender.
steps.look: A fork slides easily into a potato chunk.

steps.text: While the curry simmers, add {qty:water} of water to the rice. Bring it to a boil over high heat with the lid off. Then turn the heat to low, put the lid on, and cook without lifting the lid.
steps.tip: When the timer rings, turn off the burner and leave the lid on. The rice keeps steaming until you're ready.

steps.text: Melt the butter in the skillet over medium-low heat. Whisk in the flour to make a roux. Keep stirring, scraping the whole pan, as it slowly turns from pale to light brown.
steps.look: The color of peanut butter, smelling nutty and toasty.
steps.tip: Don't walk away. Once it starts browning, it moves fast.

steps.text: Turn off the heat under the skillet. Stir in the curry powder for about 30 seconds, until it smells strong and warm.
Ladle about a cup of broth from the curry pot into the skillet and whisk until it's a smooth, thick paste.
steps.tip: It will sizzle and steam when the broth hits the pan. Pour slowly and keep your face back.

steps.text: Scrape the curry paste into the pot and stir it in. Add the ketchup, soy sauce, and honey. Simmer with the lid off, stirring the bottom often, until it's thick and glossy.
steps.look: Thick enough to coat a spoon, and smooth.

steps.text: Fish out the thickest piece of chicken and slide the thermometer into it. It needs to read at least 165°F. If it doesn't, simmer 3 more minutes and check again.
Turn off the stove. Fluff the rice with the fork, spoon it onto one side of each plate, and ladle the curry beside it.
steps.tip: Taste the curry first, after letting it cool on the spoon. Add a pinch of salt or a little honey if it needs it.
